paragraphs: Stein variational gradient descent, or SVGD, approximates a probability distribution using a collection of particles. This paper addresses how accurately that collection can represent the target when the number of particles is finite. It provides what the authors identify as the first convergence rate explicitly covering this finite-particle setting.

The result requires a sub-Gaussian target distribution with a Lipschitz score, together with an appropriate sequence of step sizes. Under those conditions, the bound on kernel Stein discrepancy approaches zero at order 1/sqrt(log log n), where n is the particle count. The guarantee concerns this particular measure of discrepancy and depends on the stated distributional and algorithmic conditions.

The contribution makes the dependence on particle count explicit through a non-asymptotic proof. The resulting rate improves very slowly as particles are added. The authors suspect that a better dependence on n is possible, but do not establish it here; they present their proof strategy as a potential foundation for sharper results.
neurips-2023-a-finite-particle-convergen.tldr: The paper establishes a finite-particle convergence rate for SVGD under explicit assumptions on the target distribution and step sizes.

paragraphs: Semantic segmentation requires assigning a class to each pixel, making detailed annotation expensive. This paper changes the question posed to an annotator: for an informative local region, such as a superpixel, identify every class present. The answer records class presence without requiring the annotator to draw each class boundary within that region.

This query reduces annotation effort but leaves ambiguity for training. Every pixel receives a set of possible classes, rather than one definitive label. The proposed method handles this in two stages. First, it trains directly on the partial labels using two losses motivated by partial label learning and multiple instance learning. It then generates pixel-level pseudo labels and uses them for supervised training.

The authors also introduce an acquisition function tailored to selecting regions for this form of annotation. On Cityscapes and PASCAL VOC 2012, the complete approach outperforms previous work while using less annotation cost. The finding supports designing the annotation query and learning procedure together: cheaper labels become useful when the training algorithm explicitly resolves their ambiguity.
neurips-2023-active-learning-for-semanti.tldr: Asking which classes occur in selected image regions enables cheaper segmentation annotation when paired with training that resolves pixel-level ambiguity.

paragraphs: Answering logical queries over an incomplete knowledge graph requires combining evidence about relationships that may be missing. Existing approaches can reuse neural link predictors for this purpose, reducing training requirements and supporting interpretable answers. However, scores learned for individual links are not necessarily calibrated to work together in a complex query.

The proposed CQD adaptation model addresses that mismatch while keeping the original link predictor frozen. A small component learns to recalibrate its scores for complex query answering, adding only 0.03% to the model's parameter count. This calibration also enables queries containing atomic negations, expanding the forms of reasoning supported by the approach.

Across the reported datasets and query types, average Mean Reciprocal Rank rises from 34.4 to 35.1 while training uses at most 30% of available query types. The method also achieves competitive results using only 1% of complex training queries and shows robustness in out-of-domain evaluations. These findings support adapting an existing predictor's scores as a data-efficient route to more capable logical query answering.
neurips-2023-adapting-neural-link-predic.tldr: A small calibration component adapts frozen neural link predictors for more accurate, data-efficient complex query answering, including atomic negation.

paragraphs: This paper separates two sources of unequal model performance across population groups. Aleatoric discrimination arises from the data distribution, while epistemic discrimination comes from choices made during model development. The distinction provides a way to ask how much a fairness intervention improves a model relative to what the available data permits.

The authors characterize performance limits under fairness constraints while assuming perfect knowledge of the data distribution. They use Blackwell's results on comparing statistical experiments to describe the aleatoric component. Epistemic discrimination is then measured through the gap between a fairness-constrained model's accuracy and that distribution-dependent limit. This makes the reference point explicit when judging an intervention.

Applied to existing fairness methods, the analysis indicates that leading interventions effectively remove epistemic discrimination on the standard tabular datasets studied. The authors describe these datasets as overused. Their investigation of missing values also finds substantial room for improvement in handling aleatoric discrimination. The findings distinguish progress in model development from fairness risks associated with the information present in the data.
neurips-2023-aleatoric-and-epistemic-dis.tldr: The paper separates discrimination tied to the data distribution from discrimination introduced during model development to assess fairness interventions against explicit performance limits.

paragraphs: Concept Bottleneck Models make predictions through representations intended to correspond to human-understandable concepts. This can make a model easier to inspect, but the learned representations may capture irrelevant information and damage predictive performance. The paper proposes a cooperative Concept Bottleneck Model, or coop-CBM, to improve the usefulness of these concept representations.

The authors emphasize that the resulting representations are particularly meaningful when fine-grained concept labels are unavailable. They also introduce a concept orthogonal loss. This additional training objective encourages different concept representations to separate while reducing distances within a concept. Its purpose is to organize the representation so that concepts are more distinct and internally consistent.

Experiments cover image classification on CUB, AwA2, CelebA, and TIL, together with several distributional shift settings. The authors report higher accuracy in every shift setting they evaluate, including comparisons with black-box models having the highest concept accuracy. These results suggest that improving how concepts are represented can support both transparency and predictive performance when the evaluated data distribution changes.
neurips-2023-auxiliary-losses-for-learni.tldr: Coop-CBM uses auxiliary training objectives to improve concept representations and achieves higher accuracy across the evaluated distribution shifts.

paragraphs: This paper introduces a solver for regularized optimal transport, focusing on both computational efficiency and flexibility in the choice of regularizer. Its central design uses Douglas-Rachford splitting. The authors develop this technique into an algorithm that can handle a broad class of regularizers, making the solver applicable across multiple versions of the optimization problem.

The method combines strong global convergence guarantees with inexpensive iterations and support for GPU parallelization. These properties address complementary concerns: the convergence analysis establishes the algorithm's behavior, while the iteration cost and parallel execution affect how quickly it can run. The reported advantage therefore involves both mathematical guarantees and a computational design suited to GPU hardware.

The authors report that the solver is considerably faster than leading methods on many problems and demonstrate its competitiveness in domain adaptation and generative-model learning. The scope of that speed claim is many problems, rather than every possible use. Together, the results support a practical solver that combines regularizer flexibility, convergence guarantees, and efficient computation.
neurips-2023-bringing-regularized-optima.tldr: A GPU-friendly Douglas-Rachford solver supports a broad class of regularized optimal transport problems with global convergence guarantees and reported speed improvements.

paragraphs: Imitation learning can fail when it ignores the causal mechanisms behind observed behavior. This paper investigates what becomes possible when the learner also knows context-specific independence relations. These are relationships in which variables are independent only under particular circumstances, providing causal information that a description without those contexts would overlook.

The authors first show that deciding whether imitation is feasible with this information is NP-hard. They then derive a necessary graphical criterion: successful imitation requires the causal structure to satisfy this condition. Under an additional structural assumption, they prove that the same criterion is sufficient. The assumption matters because the unrestricted necessity result alone does not establish feasibility.

Finally, the paper proposes a sound algorithmic approach that uses both the known independence relations and observed data. Its contribution connects additional causal knowledge to concrete feasibility tests and a learning procedure. The results also expose a computational challenge: more detailed causal information can help formulate imitation, while deciding feasibility remains difficult in the general setting studied.
neurips-2023-causal-imitability-under-co.tldr: Known context-specific independences enable new causal imitation criteria and a sound algorithm, although deciding feasibility is NP-hard in general.

paragraphs: Contextual decision-making requires selecting an action using information about the current situation. A model must capture how rewards depend on that context and the decision, often while expressing uncertainty about its predictions. This paper addresses the difficulty of obtaining accurate approximation and explicit uncertainty estimates within the same surrogate model.

The proposed neural network-accompanied Gaussian process, or NN-AGP, assigns complementary roles to two model types. Neural networks approximate potentially complicated dependence on contextual variables. A Gaussian process models the decision variable and supplies explicit uncertainty quantification. This division is the central design choice: the contextual component provides expressive approximation, while the decision component retains Gaussian-process uncertainty.

The authors analyze the model's maximum information gain and prove regret bounds for the associated algorithms. They also report improved approximation compared with existing approaches and evaluate effectiveness on synthetic and practical problems. The contribution therefore combines a modeling strategy with theoretical analysis and empirical evidence, supporting its use for decisions where both reward prediction and uncertainty matter.
neurips-2023-contextual-gaussian-process.tldr: NN-AGP combines neural modeling of context with Gaussian-process modeling of decisions to support accurate reward prediction and explicit uncertainty estimates.

paragraphs: DataComp makes dataset construction a controlled research task for multimodal learning. It starts with a candidate pool of 12.8 billion image-text pairs from Common Crawl. Participants develop filtering methods or introduce curated data sources, then assess the resulting datasets through a shared training and evaluation workflow.

The workflow uses standardized CLIP training code and evaluates trained models on 38 downstream test sets. Multiple compute scales span four orders of magnitude, allowing researchers with different resources to participate and study scaling behavior. Keeping the training procedure standardized helps researchers examine how dataset choices affect the resulting model's performance.

The strongest reported baseline, DataComp-1B, trains a CLIP ViT-L/14 from scratch to 79.2% zero-shot ImageNet accuracy. This exceeds OpenAI's CLIP ViT-L/14 by 3.7 percentage points using the same training procedure and compute. The result provides concrete evidence that dataset design can yield substantial improvements within a fixed training setup. The broader contribution is a reusable testbed for comparing data curation decisions systematically.
neurips-2023-datacomp-in-search-of-the-n.tldr: DataComp standardizes multimodal dataset experiments and demonstrates improved CLIP performance through data curation at the same training compute.

paragraphs: DISCOVER aims to explain the functions of individual neurons in vision networks through text descriptions. It builds on network dissection, which investigates what a trained network's internal units represent. The goal is to make the network's decision process easier to examine by connecting active neurons to understandable input characteristics.

The framework combines multimodal vision-text models with layers that use stochastic local competition among linear units. For a particular input, only a small fraction of neurons activate, with reported activation levels as low as approximately 4%. The inferred activation patterns encourage neurons to specialize in inputs with particular characteristics, diversifying their individual functions.

This sparse activity makes the dissection process more manageable because descriptions are generated for the few active neurons. Experiments show that the resulting vision networks retain or improve classification performance while supporting textual examination of their representations. The finding supports the compatibility of selective neuron activation, predictive performance, and more accessible inspection of internal behavior in the evaluated networks.
neurips-2023-discover-making-vision-netw.tldr: DISCOVER combines sparse competitive neuron activation with vision-text models to describe internal functions while retaining or improving classification performance.

paragraphs: EMBERSim addresses a shortage of data for studying similarity between binary files. The authors observe that available research often focuses on similarity among malware and pays less attention to clean files. They argue that this imbalance matters for detection bypass, making a broader treatment of file similarity important for security research.

The project builds on EMBER, an existing malware classification dataset, by adding similarity information and similarity-informed tags. It also adds automatically determined malware class tags. Those class labels are produced using the open-source AVClass tool with VirusTotal data, giving researchers another way to organize and investigate the files.

The contribution includes both the augmented databank and shared implementations of a class scoring technique and a leaf similarity method. Its main outcome is research infrastructure for examining relationships between files, beyond their classification as malicious or clean. By combining similarity annotations, malware classes, and accompanying methods, EMBERSim supplies material for further work on a previously underserved research problem.
neurips-2023-embersim-a-large-scale-data.tldr: EMBERSim augments EMBER with similarity information, automated malware class tags, and shared methods to support binary-file similarity research.

paragraphs: Smooth target functions can make statistical learning less vulnerable to high input dimensionality. This paper examines when a dataset is large enough to benefit from that smoothness. The motivating concern is that useful estimates of higher-order derivatives seem to require observations close together, which can be difficult when the sample count is small relative to dimension.

The authors derive new lower bounds on generalization error to formalize this concern. Lower bounds describe limits on achievable accuracy, making them a way to investigate whether the available samples support the benefits associated with smoothness. The analysis connects the mathematical regularity of a target function to the practical availability of informative observations.

The paper also examines constants and transitional regimes that classical learning-theory statements often leave in the background. These aspects can dominate behavior at practically relevant sample sizes. Its contribution is to sharpen the question of when smoothness becomes useful, bringing attention to the finite-data regime between a theoretical advantage and its realization in a learning problem.
neurips-2023-how-many-samples-are-needed.tldr: New generalization-error lower bounds examine how much data is needed before target-function smoothness can deliver its expected learning benefits.

paragraphs: People responding to the same naturalistic stimulus can differ in both where brain activity occurs and how it unfolds over time. Existing alignment approaches described in the paper handle spatial differences while assuming exact temporal correspondence, or handle temporal differences while assuming exact spatial correspondence. Hyper-HMM jointly addresses both kinds of variation.

The model learns a linear projection from brain voxels into a lower-dimensional latent space. Within that space, it divides activity over time into corresponding events. This allows each individual's progression through an event sequence to be tracked while also aligning representations across people. The same framework can incorporate another feature space, such as the semantic content of a stimulus.

Using fMRI recordings of students watching lecture videos, the authors align participants and the videos' semantic content in a common low-dimensional space. The learned mappings also generalize to held-out data. These findings support studying shared event structure together with individual temporal trajectories, providing a way to examine cognitive dynamics during complex stimuli.
neurips-2023-hyper-hmm-aligning-human-br.tldr: Hyper-HMM jointly aligns spatial brain patterns and temporal events, connecting individual fMRI responses with lecture-video semantics in a shared latent space.

paragraphs: Federated learning must contend with differences between clients' training data, but it also faces changes within a client's data at test time. This paper distinguishes those two problems and asks whether the first can help address the second. Diverse training clients may contain useful information for learning features that remain stable when test inputs change.

The proposed FedICON framework uses supervised contrastive learning during each client's local training. This encourages sample-level representations that capture invariant information. Global aggregation then combines learning across heterogeneous clients, aiming to strengthen that capability through their varied data. Client differences become a source of information for learning invariance.

At test time, an unsupervised contrastive-learning procedure adapts the model to incoming data. This connects the invariance learned during federated training to the distribution encountered by an individual client. The authors report extensive experiments supporting FedICON's effectiveness against feature-level test-time shifts. The evidence supports using inter-client diversity constructively within a framework that also performs explicit test-time adaptation.
neurips-2023-is-heterogeneity-notorious-.tldr: FedICON uses contrastive learning across heterogeneous clients and at test time to improve adaptation to feature-level distribution shifts.

paragraphs: Unsupervised domain adaptation transfers learning from labeled source data to unlabeled target data. A major obstacle is that source labels may correlate with environmental features that do not remain reliable in the target domain. The paper argues that using target samples mainly as auxiliary training data can overlook distributional clues that expose those misleading relationships.

Invariant Consistency Learning, or ICON, gives source and target domains equal status in learning a classifier. Predictions must agree with source labels and with clusters in the target data. This joint requirement uses the target distribution's own structure to rule out spurious correlations that are inconsistent there, rather than relying solely on supervision inherited from the source.

The authors report state-of-the-art results on Office-Home and VisDA-2017, along with performance exceeding all conventional methods on WILDS 2.0. These findings support treating unlabeled target structure as a direct learning constraint. The central contribution is the consistency requirement linking labeled source examples and target clusters within one invariant classifier.
neurips-2023-make-the-u-in-uda-matter-in.tldr: ICON aligns predictions with source labels and target clusters to counter spurious correlations and improve unsupervised domain adaptation.

paragraphs: A world model predicts how a system may evolve under different actions. For longer forecasts, the challenge includes representing behavior at several temporal scales and estimating uncertainty about future states. This paper introduces a probabilistic framework designed to learn those different levels of temporal abstraction within one model.

The proposed Multi Time Scale State Space model, or MTS3, uses a computationally efficient inference scheme operating across multiple time scales. The authors describe it as producing accurate long-horizon predictions together with uncertainty estimates several seconds into the future. Modeling at multiple scales is therefore tied directly to the task of forecasting extended action-dependent behavior.

Experiments focus on predicting future dynamics conditional on actions. They cover several system identification benchmarks, including complex simulated systems and real-world dynamical systems, where MTS3 outperforms recent methods. These results support the model's forecasting capability in the evaluated settings. The contribution combines a probabilistic representation of multiple temporal scales with an inference procedure intended to make that representation computationally practical.
neurips-2023-multi-time-scale-world-mode.tldr: MTS3 models dynamics across multiple time scales to improve action-conditioned long-horizon predictions and provide uncertainty estimates.

paragraphs: This paper studies statistics built by applying a function to pairs of users' inputs and aggregating the results. Such quantities depend on relationships between observations, so the computational target extends beyond a summary of separate individual contributions. The authors investigate how to calculate these pairwise summaries under differential privacy in the local model.

The formulation covers several familiar measures, including Kendall's tau, Area Under Curve, Gini's mean difference, and Gini's entropy. Treating them as instances of a shared pairwise problem allows the work to address a family of statistics together. The particular function applied to each pair determines which quantity the computation estimates.

The authors contribute several new generic algorithms, drawing on techniques developed for differentially private linear queries. The methodological contribution is this connection between tools for linear queries and the problem of private pairwise computation. It provides algorithmic approaches that apply across the stated formulation, making the work relevant to multiple statistical quantities under the same local privacy setting.
neurips-2023-on-computing-pairwise-stati.tldr: The paper develops generic locally differentially private algorithms for pairwise statistics using techniques from private linear-query computation.

paragraphs: Choosing between clustering results depends on how their similarity is measured. This paper identifies tradeoffs in established comparison metrics: Adjusted Rand Index and Adjusted Mutual Information have type II bias, while Standardized Mutual Information removes that bias but suffers from counterintuitive non-monotonic behavior and high computational cost.

The authors introduce the p-value adjusted Rand Index, called PMI_2. They establish that it is type II unbiased and provably monotonic, presenting it as the first cluster comparison method to combine these properties. They also develop fast approximations that outperform Standardized Mutual Information, addressing the computational burden alongside the metric's statistical behavior.

Synthetic benchmarks examine unbiased clustering selection, approximation quality, and runtime efficiency. Experiments on image and social-network datasets show how the metric can help select better clustering and community-detection algorithms. The contribution matters because the comparison rule itself can influence which method a practitioner chooses. PMI_2 provides a theoretically supported alternative whose practical approximations are also evaluated.
neurips-2023-p-value-adjustment-for-mono.tldr: PMI_2 combines type II unbiased clustering comparison with proven monotonicity and fast approximations for practical algorithm selection.

paragraphs: This paper studies how a theoretical universal reinforcement-learning agent can obtain good policies through learning. Its reference point is AIXI, which relies primarily on comprehensive planning search to identify an optimal policy. The authors define an alternative agent, Self-AIXI, that places self-prediction at the center of policy learning.

Self-AIXI predicts its own stream of actions. That stream is generated by selecting actions that maximize its current on-policy Q-value estimates, using a universal mixture policy. The authors relate this action-generation mechanism to TD(0) agents. The design connects the agent's present value estimates, its resulting actions, and the learning process that predicts those actions.

The main results are theoretical: Self-AIXI converges to AIXI and inherits properties including maximal Legg-Hutter intelligence and self-optimization. This establishes a formal connection between the proposed learning-centered agent and the planning-centered reference. The significance lies in demonstrating that self-prediction can underpin an alternative universal-agent construction with these stated properties, extending the theoretical picture of how learning and planning relate.
neurips-2023-self-predictive-universal-a.tldr: Self-AIXI learns by predicting its own actions and is proved to converge to AIXI while inheriting key theoretical intelligence properties.

paragraphs: Model-based reinforcement learning trains an agent using trajectories imagined by a learned world model. This reduces dependence on additional interaction with the real environment, but model errors can lead an agent toward behavior that succeeds only in simulation. The paper motivates stochastic modeling as a useful ingredient when the learned environment cannot be perfectly accurate.

STORM combines a Transformer's sequence-modeling and generation capabilities with the stochastic structure of a variational autoencoder. The architecture is designed to provide an efficient world model for reinforcement learning from visual inputs. Its central contribution is this combination of expressive temporal modeling and randomness within the learned simulator.

On Atari 100k, STORM reports mean performance of 126.7% of human performance, a record among the compared state-of-the-art methods without lookahead search. Training with experience corresponding to 1.85 hours of real-time interaction takes 4.3 hours on a single NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3090. These results support both the agent's benchmark performance and the computational efficiency of the reported training setup.
neurips-2023-storm-efficient-stochastic-.tldr: STORM combines Transformers and stochastic latent modeling to achieve strong Atari 100k performance with efficient single-GPU training.

paragraphs: Understanding how a model responds to changes in its training data can reveal useful information about its behavior. Measuring that sensitivity can be difficult and expensive, especially while training is still underway. This paper introduces the Memory-Perturbation Equation, or MPE, to express the relationship between data perturbations and model sensitivity.

The equation is derived from Bayesian principles. The authors use it to unify existing sensitivity measures, extend them across a wide variety of models and algorithms, and expose useful properties of sensitivity. This common formulation provides a framework for studying measures that might otherwise be treated separately for different learning procedures.

Empirically, the authors find that sensitivity estimates collected during training can faithfully predict generalization to unseen test data. This connects a quantity observed during optimization to performance beyond the training set. The finding is an experimental result, while applications to robust and adaptive learning are presented as an expectation for future research. The contribution combines that demonstrated predictive use with a broader mathematical framework.
neurips-2023-the-memory-perturbation-equ.tldr: The Memory-Perturbation Equation unifies data-sensitivity measures, with experiments showing that training-time estimates can predict test generalization.

paragraphs: Graph neural networks produce predictions for connected data, but reliable deployment also requires knowing how uncertain those predictions are. This paper introduces conformalized GNNs, which return prediction sets or intervals with a specified coverage probability. The aim is to accompany a prediction with a statistically grounded account of which outcomes remain plausible.

The authors establish a permutation-invariance condition that enables conformal prediction to remain valid on graph data and characterize test-time coverage exactly. They also investigate how non-conformity scores relate to network structure. That connection motivates a topology-aware correction model, which updates predictions to make the resulting sets or intervals smaller while maintaining valid coverage.

Experiments achieve the requested marginal coverage levels and reduce prediction-set or interval size by up to 74% relative to the baselines. Smaller outputs make the uncertainty estimates more informative at the same coverage target. The method also shows satisfactory conditional coverage across raw and network features empirically; that finding is distinct from the formal coverage guarantee established under the paper's condition.
neurips-2023-uncertainty-quantification-.tldr: CF-GNN extends conformal uncertainty estimates to graphs and uses topology-aware correction to produce smaller prediction sets while preserving target marginal coverage.

paragraphs: Learning from explanations uses human guidance about relevant or irrelevant input features to shape how a model makes predictions. Existing methods described in this paper align human explanations with local model interpretations. The authors argue that these methods require strong model smoothing, which can lead to suboptimal predictive performance.

The paper reframes explanation-based learning as a robustness problem. Human explanations define a lower-dimensional manifold from which input perturbations can be drawn. Those perturbations turn the explanation into a structured robustness requirement. The authors show theoretically and empirically how this formulation alleviates the need for strong smoothing, providing another way to incorporate human guidance into training.

Several approaches to achieving the required robustness improve performance over earlier explanation-based methods. Combining robustness with an existing method produces state-of-the-art results on the synthetic and real-world benchmarks studied. The findings support using explanations to specify meaningful perturbations, with the training procedure learning from how predictions should behave under those changes. The contribution includes both this reformulation and evidence for its practical benefit.
neurips-2023-use-perturbations-when-lear.tldr: Human explanations can define robustness-oriented perturbations that reduce reliance on strong model smoothing and improve explanation-guided learning.

paragraphs: VisIT-Bench evaluates how well vision-language models follow instructions across a broad range of envisioned real-world uses. It contains 592 test queries organized around 70 instruction families, covering tasks from recognition to game playing and creative generation. This breadth makes the evaluation sensitive to more than basic image-question answering.

Each query includes a human-written caption tailored to its instruction. For a question about wheelchair access, for example, the description highlights ramps and possible obstacles. These captions make the relevant visual information explicit. They support human-verified reference responses and enable a text-only language model to evaluate multimodal answers in a way that aligns with human judgments.

Both human and automatic evaluations reveal quality gaps between tested models and reference responses. The strongest instruction-following model wins against the GPT-4 reference in only 27% of comparisons. That is a comparative preference result, rather than an overall task-accuracy score. The benchmark also accepts model-response submissions through its website, providing a continuing mechanism for evaluating additional systems.
neurips-2023-visit-bench-a-dynamic-bench.tldr: VisIT-Bench uses instruction-specific visual descriptions to evaluate diverse vision-language tasks and reveals substantial gaps between tested models and reference responses.

paragraphs: VPP addresses conditional 3D generation, where inputs such as text or images guide the creation of a shape. The paper examines how the choice of 3D representation affects generation quality, speed, and the tasks a model can support. Its solution progressively combines a structured voxel representation with a sparse point representation.

A Voxel Semantic Generator uses the structured voxel representation, while a Point Upsampler uses the sparsity of unstructured points. This pairing supports efficient generation across multiple object categories. The architecture also includes a masked-generation Transformer, allowing the approach to serve generation, editing, completion, and pre-training tasks.

The authors report generating high-quality 8K point clouds in 0.2 seconds. Their experiments show high-fidelity, diverse shapes across different categories, together with strong representation-transfer performance. These findings support the progressive representation as a way to combine efficient generation with broader downstream utility. The contribution centers on coordinating complementary 3D representations within one generation pipeline, with the reported results demonstrating both speed and versatility.
neurips-2023-vpp-efficient-conditional-3.tldr: VPP progressively combines voxel and point representations to generate diverse 3D shapes efficiently and support editing, completion, and pre-training.
